name: Microsoft Certified: Information Security Administrator Associate
title: Practice Exam 3
note: Microsoft scores SC-401 on a 1–1000 scale with 700 to pass. This practice exam reports a straight percentage; treat 80% as your readiness bar.

cs.title: Case Study — Litware Inc (Technology Company)
cs.body:
Litware Inc is a technology company with 3,000 employees on Microsoft 365 E5.

• Developer-heavy workforce; GitHub repositories connected to Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
• SharePoint Online used for project documentation and design specifications
• BYOD allowed for managers — iOS and Android devices enrolled in Microsoft Intune
• Microsoft 365 Copilot deployed for all 200 managers
• GDPR compliance required — EU customer personal data is processed and stored in M365

yn.title: Yes / No
yn.body:
Litware has Microsoft 365 E5 licenses. The compliance admin reviews this PowerShell command:

    Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate 05/01/2026 -EndDate 05/20/2026 -RecordType SharePointFileOperation -Operations FileAccessed

Litware also has a 5-year custom SharePoint retention policy and a default 90-day org-wide retention policy applied to the same SharePoint locations.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true or No if it is false.

questions.stem: Managers use BYOD devices (enrolled in Intune) to access SharePoint project sites from personal browsers. Litware wants to prevent file downloads and printing from these unmanaged browser sessions without blocking read access entirely. Which configuration achieves this?
options: A DLP policy blocking SharePoint downloads from devices not enrolled in Intune
A sensitivity label with Assign permissions now encryption applied to all files in the SharePoint site
A container sensitivity label applied to the SharePoint site, configured to restrict unmanaged devices to web-only access (no download, no print)
A conditional access policy requiring full Intune compliance before any SharePoint access is permitted
questions.explanation: C is correct. Container sensitivity labels on SharePoint sites include an 'Unmanaged devices' setting with three options: block access, allow limited web-only access (view, no download/print/sync), or allow full access. Web-only meets both requirements — read access is preserved while download/print/sync are blocked for unmanaged sessions. The configuration leverages Entra ID Conditional Access App Control but is set directly on the container label. A is wrong because SharePoint DLP does not have a device-state condition — distinguishing managed from unmanaged is conditional access territory. B is wrong because file-level encryption applies uniformly regardless of device — it doesn't selectively limit download from BYOD. D is wrong because requiring Intune compliance for ANY access fully blocks BYOD, contradicting the requirement to preserve read access.

questions.stem: When a Litware employee account is deleted, their OneDrive contained project files covered by an active 5-year retention policy. What happens to the OneDrive content?
options: Content is immediately deleted with the user account
Content is preserved for 30 days and then deleted per the standard account deletion process
Content remains preserved for the full 5-year retention period in the Preservation Hold Library
Content is automatically transferred to the deleted employee manager OneDrive account
questions.explanation: C is correct. Retention policies survive account deletion. OneDrive content covered by an active retention policy is preserved in the Preservation Hold Library for the full policy duration, regardless of the user account being removed. A is wrong because retention policy explicitly prevents immediate deletion. B is wrong because the standard 30-day OneDrive retention applies only when no retention policy is in effect. D is wrong because Microsoft does not auto-transfer OneDrive content to the manager — that would require a separate offboarding step and is not driven by retention policy.

questions.stem: Litware CISO wants a dashboard showing which project documents Copilot is accessing, whether they are sensitivity labeled, and whether sensitive unlabeled content is being surfaced to Copilot users. Which solution provides this visibility?
options: Microsoft Defender XDR — Advanced Hunting with CopilotInteraction event type queries
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management scoped to Copilot-enabled users
Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI
Microsoft Entra ID audit logs filtered for Microsoft 365 Copilot service principal activity
questions.explanation: C (DSPM for AI) is correct. Data Security Posture Management for AI is the purpose-built Purview solution for Copilot governance visibility — sensitivity label coverage on content accessed by Copilot, oversharing risk on broadly accessible/unlabeled content, and AI interaction activity metrics. A is wrong because Defender XDR Advanced Hunting can query CopilotInteraction audit events but does not provide the dashboard-level governance view that DSPM for AI does. B is wrong because IRM detects user RISK behaviors, not Copilot content exposure. D is wrong because Entra ID audit logs show sign-in/service activity, not Copilot content access or labeling exposure.

questions.stem: Litware must detect full names of EU residents in SharePoint documents to comply with GDPR data subject rights requests. Names include many European cultural variations. Which SIT provides the best detection?
options: A custom regex SIT with patterns matching common European name formats
A keyword list SIT populated with employee names extracted from the HR database
The All Full Names named entity SIT using ML-based detection across cultural name variations
An EDM classifier mapping names to a GDPR data subject registry maintained in SQL
questions.explanation: C (All Full Names) is correct. It is a named entity SIT using machine learning to detect person names across European, Asian, Middle Eastern, and other naming conventions without relying on fixed patterns. Ideal for GDPR scenarios where name formats vary widely across EU member states. A is wrong because no general 'European name format' regex can capture the cultural variation — and named entity SITs were specifically built to solve this. B is wrong because a keyword list from HR captures only employees, not all EU residents in customer data. D is wrong because building an EDM classifier of every EU subject's name is operationally infeasible and unnecessary when a named entity SIT does the job.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label Confidential has its header text changed from CONFIDENTIAL to CONFIDENTIAL — LITWARE INC in the Purview portal. When does the updated header appear on a previously labeled document?
options: Immediately — as soon as the label configuration is saved in the Purview compliance portal
The next time a user opens and saves the document in an Office application
Only when the user manually removes and re-applies the label to the document
Within 1 hour — as the label policy synchronizes to all Office applications automatically
questions.explanation: B is correct. Visual-marking changes (headers, footers, watermarks) on sensitivity labels take effect the next time a user opens and re-saves a labeled document in an Office application. Previously saved files do not retroactively update — the document must be re-opened and saved in Office after the updated label policy has propagated to the client (typically within an hour). A is wrong because the change is not applied immediately to previously saved documents — only on next save. C is wrong because manual remove-and-re-apply is not required; a normal save is enough. D is wrong because policy synchronization within an hour delivers the new label DEFINITION to Office, but the document itself still needs to be saved to receive the updated markings.

questions.stem: A compliance officer needs to determine what percentage of SharePoint documents are currently labeled versus unlabeled across the entire tenant. Which Microsoft Purview tool provides this inventory?
options: Activity Explorer — shows labeling change events sorted by date
Microsoft Purview Audit — filter for SensitivityLabelApplied operations across the tenant
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager — data classification control assessment
Content Explorer — provides a current inventory of items by sensitivity label, SIT, and location
questions.explanation: D is correct. Content Explorer provides the current inventory of labeled and sensitive items across SharePoint, Exchange, and OneDrive — filtered by label, SIT, or location. You can view item counts per label and identify coverage gaps. A (Activity Explorer) is wrong because it shows the HISTORY of labeling events, not the current state. B (Audit) is wrong because audit captures discrete events; aggregating into a tenant-wide inventory is what Content Explorer is for. C (Compliance Manager) is wrong because Compliance Manager tracks regulatory control implementation, not current label inventory.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the scope of the MPIP Scanner versus Microsoft Purview cloud auto-labeling policies?
options: Both the MPIP Scanner and cloud auto-labeling policies can label content in SharePoint Online and on-premises file shares
The MPIP Scanner labels on-premises file shares and SharePoint Server; cloud auto-labeling policies label Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and OneDrive for Business
Cloud auto-labeling is a superset of MPIP Scanner — the Scanner is only needed for EDM classification, not for actual labeling
The MPIP Scanner operates on Windows and macOS devices; cloud auto-labeling covers Linux servers and cloud storage
questions.explanation: B is correct. MPIP Scanner targets on-premises Windows file shares and SharePoint Server (on-premises). Cloud auto-labeling policies target Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and OneDrive for Business (the Microsoft 365 cloud). The two are complementary; neither covers the other's scope. A is wrong because they have distinct, non-overlapping scopes — the Scanner doesn't touch SPO and auto-labeling doesn't touch on-prem shares. C is wrong because cloud auto-labeling cannot label on-premises content, and the Scanner is more than an EDM tool — it applies any configured sensitivity label. D is wrong because the Scanner is not a Windows/macOS client agent — it is a server-side service.

questions.stem: Your financial services organization needs to detect potentially non-compliant investment advice and conflicts of interest in employee email and Teams messages. Which Communication Compliance policy template is designed for this scenario?
options: Offensive language — uses classifiers to detect harassment, threats, and discriminatory content
Sensitive information — detects messages containing sensitive information types such as credit card numbers or SSNs
Regulatory compliance — uses classifiers trained to detect financial regulatory language and potential policy violations
Custom policy — no built-in template covers financial regulatory compliance scenarios
questions.explanation: C is correct. The Regulatory compliance template in Communication Compliance uses ML classifiers trained on financial-regulatory language — detecting potential insider-trading indicators, Reg FD violations, fiduciary conflicts, and inappropriate investment advice. Financial-services firms should use this template as a starting point. A (Offensive language) is wrong because it targets harassment/discrimination, not regulatory matters. B (Sensitive information) is wrong because it detects structured DATA types (SSNs, credit cards), not regulatory content. D is wrong because a built-in regulatory compliance template DOES exist — a custom policy isn't required as the starting point.

questions.stem: Litware needs a second OME branding configuration for the Legal department, in addition to the existing corporate OME branding. Which PowerShell cmdlet creates a NEW OME branding template?
options: Set-OMEConfiguration — modifies the existing default template with new branding settings
New-OMEConfiguration — creates a new additional OME branding configuration template
Add-OMETemplate — appends branding elements to the existing default configuration
New-TransportRule with -ApplyOMETemplate — creates both the template and transport rule simultaneously
questions.explanation: B (New-OMEConfiguration) is correct. Set-OMEConfiguration only modifies the existing default OME template. New-OMEConfiguration creates an entirely new, separate OME branding configuration; multiple OME configurations can coexist in a tenant and are referenced from transport rules via the -ApplyOMETemplate parameter. A (Set-OMEConfiguration) is wrong because Set modifies the default, not creates a new template. C (Add-OMETemplate) is wrong because no such cmdlet exists. D is wrong because New-TransportRule creates the rule but does not create OME templates — the template must already exist before the rule references it.

questions.stem: A Confidential sensitivity label includes a watermark configured in the label settings. A user prints a document with this label applied. Where does the watermark appear on the printed output?
options: The watermark appears only on screen — sensitivity label watermarks do not appear on printed output
The watermark is embedded in the document rendering and appears on printed pages
The watermark appears only on printed output from Windows — macOS printing omits watermarks
The watermark appears only on the first page — subsequent pages require a separate label configuration
questions.explanation: B is correct. Sensitivity-label watermarks are inserted as document content — they appear both on screen AND in printed output across platforms. They are rendered as part of the document, not as a DRM-style screen overlay. A is wrong because watermarks DO appear on print. C is wrong because watermarks render on macOS prints as well — they are not OS-specific. D is wrong because watermarks repeat across pages, not just the first.

questions.stem: Which content marking types can a sensitivity label apply to a document?
options: Header text, footer text, and watermark text
Header text, footer text, watermark text, and a digital signature stamp
Watermark only — headers and footers are controlled by the document template settings
Header text and watermark only — footer text is not supported as a content marking
questions.explanation: A is correct. Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels support exactly three content-marking types: header text (top of pages), footer text (bottom of pages), and watermark text (diagonal overlay on each page). B is wrong because sensitivity labels do not insert a digital signature stamp as a content marking — the markings are limited to three text-based types. C is wrong because headers AND footers ARE supported in addition to watermarks. D is wrong because footer text IS a supported marking type.

questions.stem: In a sensitive information type (SIT), what is the purpose of a supporting element?
options: It defines the data format that the primary element regex pattern must match
It provides corroborating evidence — keywords or additional patterns — that raises the confidence level when found near the primary element
It specifies which users are authorized to view content matched by the SIT in DLP reports
It links the SIT to an EDM schema for exact-data validation of the primary element
questions.explanation: B is correct. Supporting elements in a SIT (keywords, additional regex patterns, proximity conditions) provide corroborating evidence — when found near a primary-element match, they raise the confidence level (e.g., from medium to high). Without supporting elements, the primary match still fires but at a lower confidence level. A is wrong because the primary element's regex is fixed in its own configuration — supporting elements do not define it. C is wrong because RBAC governs report access, not SIT internals. D is wrong because EDM schemas are a separate SIT type — supporting elements are general SIT corroboration mechanisms.

questions.stem: You configure a service-side auto-labeling policy for SharePoint Online. The target sensitivity label uses which encryption configuration type?
options: Only labels with Let users assign permissions — service-side cannot apply pre-set permission labels
Only labels with Assign permissions now — pre-defined permissions requiring no user interaction
Both Let users assign and Assign permissions now label configurations are equally supported
Labels with no encryption only — service-side auto-labeling cannot apply any encrypted label
questions.explanation: B is correct. Service-side (cloud-based) auto-labeling can only apply labels configured with 'Assign permissions now' — because those permissions are pre-defined in the label and require no user decision at apply time. 'Let users assign permissions' requires interactive user input in an Office application and cannot be applied by an automated service-side policy. A is wrong — it reverses the relationship. C is wrong because the two encryption types are NOT equally supported by service-side auto-labeling. D is wrong because service-side auto-labeling CAN apply encrypted labels, as long as the encryption is 'Assign permissions now' type.

questions.stem: Litware must detect EU residents full names in SharePoint documents for GDPR subject rights compliance. Names include many European cultural variations. Which SIT provides the most accurate detection?
options: EU Passport Number (SIT for travel identity documents)
Person Name — English (limited to English-format name patterns only)
All Full Names (named entity SIT using ML, covering multicultural name formats)
All Personal Identifiers (a broad bundled SIT covering multiple EU personal data categories)
questions.explanation: C (All Full Names) is correct. As a named entity SIT, it uses ML to detect person names across European, Asian, Middle Eastern, and other naming conventions without depending on a fixed format — ideal for multinational GDPR scenarios. A (EU Passport Number) is wrong because it detects travel document IDs, not names. B (Person Name - English) is wrong because it is limited to English-formatted name patterns and would miss most European name variations. D is wrong because 'All Personal Identifiers' is not a real bundled SIT name in Microsoft Purview.

questions.stem: An employee notifies HR of their resignation effective in three weeks. Your organization wants IRM to immediately begin monitoring this employee for bulk downloads, USB copies, and unusual external email forwards during the notice period. Which IRM policy type should you configure?
options: Security policy violations — detects users circumventing device security controls or disabling protective software
Data leaks — general — detects sensitive content being shared broadly across the organization or externally
Data theft by departing employees — triggered by departure signals from the HR Connector and monitors exfiltration risk indicators
Offensive language in the workplace — detects policy violations in employee communications
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Data theft by departing employees' is the IRM policy template designed for this scenario. When combined with HR Connector signals about resignation/termination, it activates heightened risk scoring during the notice period — monitoring for bulk downloads, USB copies, cloud uploads, and external forwards that may indicate pre-departure exfiltration. A (Security policy violations) is wrong because it targets users disabling/circumventing endpoint controls — different signal type. B (Data leaks - general) is wrong because it covers broad sharing/exfiltration without the departure-specific risk weighting. D is wrong because it is a Communication Compliance scenario, not IRM.

questions.stem: A retention label is configured with retention period starting from When labeled. A user applies the label to a document on March 1, 2025. The document was originally created January 1, 2023. The retention period is 5 years. When does the retention period end?
options: January 1, 2028 — 5 years after the document creation date
March 1, 2030 — 5 years after the label application date
January 1, 2025 — 5 years calculated retroactively from the creation date
March 1, 2025 — the label application date itself, as retention triggers immediately
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'When labeled' starts the retention clock at the date and time the label is applied — not the creation or modification date. March 1, 2025 plus 5 years equals March 1, 2030. The January 1, 2023 creation date is irrelevant to a 'When labeled' policy. A is wrong because that uses creation date, which is a different retention-basis option. C is wrong because retroactive calculation is not how 'When labeled' works. D is wrong because retention does not expire on the day the label is applied — the clock starts then.

questions.stem: Litware is a multinational company. EU employee data must not be accessible to US-based eDiscovery managers. Which Microsoft Purview feature restricts eDiscovery search scope by organizational geography or division?
options: Information Barriers configured between EU and US organizational units
Microsoft Purview Compliance Boundaries for eDiscovery
Microsoft Entra ID administrative units limiting the search scope
Microsoft data residency commitments in the standard GDPR data protection addendum
questions.explanation: B is correct. Compliance Boundaries in Microsoft Purview eDiscovery restrict which content locations (mailboxes, SharePoint sites) an eDiscovery manager can search and hold. They are designed for organizations with multiple divisions, geographies, or subsidiaries that need eDiscovery segmentation — exactly Litware's EU vs US separation. A (Information Barriers) is wrong because IB restricts user communication, not eDiscovery search scope. C (Entra administrative units) is wrong because admin units scope Entra administrative actions, not eDiscovery scope. D is wrong because data residency commitments protect storage location but do not segment eDiscovery roles by geography.

questions.stem: What is a key advantage of using a Microsoft Purview DLP policy over an Exchange mail flow rule (transport rule) for protecting sensitive information?
options: Mail flow rules cannot apply to messages sent within the same organization; DLP policies can
DLP policies detect sensitive information across multiple workloads (Exchange, SharePoint, Teams, endpoint) using SITs; mail flow rules are limited to Exchange message attributes
DLP policies evaluate content in real time before queuing; mail flow rules evaluate content only after queuing
Mail flow rules cannot block messages; only DLP policies can enforce blocking actions on email
questions.explanation: B is correct. DLP policies use SITs (and other condition types) to detect sensitive CONTENT across multiple workloads — Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, endpoint, Power BI. Mail flow rules operate on Exchange message attributes (headers, subject, envelope, sender/recipient) and cannot inspect content for SITs. For multi-workload, content-aware protection, DLP is required. A is wrong because mail flow rules can match internal-to-internal messages. C is wrong because both technologies evaluate before final delivery — the differentiator is content awareness, not timing. D is wrong because mail flow rules CAN block messages (Reject the message); blocking is not exclusive to DLP.

questions.stem: Litware needs a custom SIT to detect any of 75,000 proprietary technology terms in documents. Standard keyword list SITs have a character limit too small for this. What SIT feature supports large keyword lists?
options: Extended keyword SIT with dynamic lookup from a SharePoint list
Keyword dictionary SIT supporting up to 1 million unique terms
A trainable classifier seeded with documents containing the 75,000 terms
An EDM SIT using a 75,000-row database table of proprietary terms
questions.explanation: B is correct. Keyword dictionaries in Microsoft Purview SITs support up to 1 million unique terms (about 1 MB of UTF-8 text). For large proprietary term lists like 75,000 technology terms, a keyword-dictionary SIT is the right choice. A is wrong because there is no 'dynamic SharePoint list lookup' SIT type. C is wrong because trainable classifiers learn content topics from examples — they are not the mechanism for matching a specific list of terms. D is wrong because EDM matches structured rows of data with primary/supporting fields — not arbitrary technology terms.

questions.stem: You want a DLP alert to be generated only when a single incident involves more than 50 sensitive items — to reduce alert fatigue from low-volume matches. Where should you configure this threshold?
options: In the sensitivity label policy alert settings for the matching label
In the DLP policy alert configuration — set the threshold to generate an alert only when the count meets or exceeds 50 items
In Microsoft Sentinel — create a custom analytics rule that filters DLP signals below the threshold
In Compliance Manager — set an incident count threshold per compliance control
questions.explanation: B is correct. DLP alert configurations include threshold settings — you can specify the minimum match count before an alert is generated. Setting a 50-item threshold means lower-volume incidents are still logged in DLP activity reports but no admin alert fires, reducing noise. A is wrong because alert thresholds are configured on the DLP policy, not on sensitivity label policy alerts. C is wrong because Sentinel is out of scope for SC-401 — it would be an over-engineered solution to a Purview-native problem. D is wrong because Compliance Manager assesses regulatory implementation, not DLP alert volumes.

questions.stem: Adaptive Protection in IRM assigns users to insider risk levels. Which risk level triggers the most restrictive DLP enforcement actions when combined with a DLP policy?
options: Minor
Moderate
Elevated
Critical
questions.explanation: C (Elevated) is correct. Adaptive Protection assigns three risk levels: Minor (lowest), Moderate, and Elevated (highest). DLP policies using the 'Insider risk level is' condition can apply tiered enforcement — Elevated typically triggers the strictest action (block), Moderate often block-with-override, Minor audit-only. D (Critical) is wrong because 'Critical' is NOT a valid Adaptive Protection level. A (Minor) and B (Moderate) are wrong because Elevated is more restrictive than both.

questions.stem: A user permanently deletes an email from their Exchange Online mailbox (purges it from Deleted Items). Where is the item stored and for how long by default?
options: The item is permanently and immediately deleted when purged from Deleted Items
The item is moved to Recoverable Items — Deletions folder and retained for 14 days by default
The item is moved to the archive mailbox Recoverable Items and retained for 90 days
The item moves to the archive mailbox immediately and is retained indefinitely
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a user purges an item from Deleted Items (Shift+Delete or empties the folder), the item moves to the hidden Recoverable Items → Deletions subfolder for 14 days by default. Litigation holds, eDiscovery holds, or retention policies extend this period — potentially indefinitely — and make the items discoverable via Content Search. A is wrong because the item is NOT immediately and permanently deleted; it goes to Recoverable Items first. C is wrong because the archive mailbox is not the default landing spot — the user's mailbox Recoverable Items is. D is wrong because items do not automatically migrate to the archive immediately, and they are not retained indefinitely without a hold.

questions.stem: A retention policy is configured with Retain only action (no delete) for a 5-year period applied to Exchange Online mailboxes. What happens to emails after the 5-year retention period ends?
options: Emails are automatically deleted by the retention policy after the 5-year period expires
Emails remain in the mailbox indefinitely — Retain only has no automatic delete component
Emails are automatically moved to the archive mailbox after 5 years
Emails are flagged for disposition review at the 5-year mark and held pending review decision
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Retain only' ensures content CANNOT be permanently deleted by users during the retention period — but it does NOT schedule deletion at period end. After the period expires, the retention protection lapses and content is simply no longer shielded by the policy. Compare with 'Retain X years, then delete,' which actively schedules disposition. A is wrong because Retain only does not auto-delete. C is wrong because Retain only does not move content to archive. D is wrong because Retain only does not trigger disposition review at period end — that requires Retain-then-delete with reviewers configured.

questions.stem: Where should a compliance administrator navigate in Microsoft Purview to create a custom audit log retention policy extending retention for specific operations to 3 years?
options: Microsoft Purview portal — Data lifecycle management — Retention policies
Microsoft Purview portal — Audit — Audit retention policies
Microsoft 365 admin center — Settings — Security and privacy — Audit
Microsoft Entra ID admin center — Monitoring — Audit logs — Retention configuration
questions.explanation: B is correct. Custom audit log retention policies are configured in the Microsoft Purview portal under Audit, then on the Retention policies tab. These are separate from data lifecycle retention policies. Audit retention policies specify which workload record types to retain, for how long, and for which users/activities. A is wrong because Data lifecycle management retention policies cover content retention (emails, files), not audit logs. C is wrong because the M365 admin center does not house audit retention policy configuration. D is wrong because Entra ID admin center handles Entra audit logs separately — not Microsoft Purview unified audit log retention.

questions.stem: A DLP alert fires for a user who also has a high-risk Entra ID sign-in alert and a suspicious process execution alert from Defender for Endpoint. In which portal are all three signals consolidated into a unified security incident automatically?
options: Microsoft Purview portal — DLP alert management dashboard
Microsoft Defender XDR portal — Incidents queue
Microsoft Entra ID portal — Risk events — Identity protection
Microsoft Sentinel — Incidents (requires individual data connector configuration for each source)
questions.explanation: B is correct. Microsoft Defender XDR automatically correlates related alerts from Microsoft Purview (DLP), Entra ID Protection (identity risk), and Defender for Endpoint (device alerts) into a single unified incident with a complete attack story. A is wrong because the Purview DLP dashboard surfaces DLP alerts only — no cross-product correlation. C is wrong because Entra ID portal handles identity-risk events but is not the consolidation point for DLP + endpoint signals. D is wrong because while Sentinel can do this, it requires manual data connector configuration per source — Defender XDR provides the correlation natively for first-party signals.

questions.stem: Adaptive Protection is enabled and a user is assigned an Elevated insider risk level. A DLP policy rule uses the condition Insider risk level is Elevated with a Block action. The user attempts to upload a file — which contains no sensitive information types — to a personal cloud storage domain. What happens?
options: The upload proceeds — the insider risk level condition is informational only and does not trigger enforcement without a matching sensitive information type
The upload is blocked — the user Elevated insider risk level alone satisfies the DLP rule condition and triggers the block action
The upload is blocked only after a second violation in the same session — the first attempt generates a warning
IRM blocks the upload directly — Adaptive Protection does not route enforcement through DLP policies
questions.explanation: B is correct. When Adaptive Protection is active, the DLP condition 'Insider risk level is' can trigger enforcement based on the user's behavioral risk level ALONE — a matching SIT is NOT required. If the user is Elevated and the DLP rule blocks for Elevated, the upload is blocked regardless of file content. This enables proactive behavior-based enforcement on high-risk users. A is wrong because the condition does enforce without a SIT match. C is wrong because there is no automatic two-strike warning behavior built into the condition. D is wrong because IRM itself does not directly block — IRM provides the risk-level signal that DLP enforces against.

questions.stem: The FileAccessed audit event in the unified audit log records which activity?
options: When a file in SharePoint is permanently deleted by a user
When a file in SharePoint or OneDrive is opened or previewed by a user
When a sensitivity label is applied to a file for the first time
When a file is checked out for exclusive editing by a user in SharePoint
questions.explanation: B is correct. FileAccessed is generated in the SharePoint and OneDrive audit log when a user opens or previews a file — capturing user identity, IP address, file name, file path, and site URL. A (file permanently deleted) is FileDeleted — different operation. C (sensitivity label applied) is SensitivityLabelApplied — different operation. D (file checked out) is CheckOut — different operation.

questions.stem: A compliance administrator wants to search unified audit logs for Teams meeting recording activity using PowerShell. Which command sequence is correct?
options: Connect-IPPSSession; then Search-UnifiedAuditLog -RecordType MicrosoftTeams
Connect-ExchangeOnline; then Search-UnifiedAuditLog -RecordType MicrosoftTeams
Connect-MgGraph; then Get-MgAuditLogSignIn -Filter recordType eq MicrosoftTeams
Connect-IPPSSession; then Get-ComplianceCase -RecordType MicrosoftTeams
questions.explanation: B is correct. Search-UnifiedAuditLog is an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet — it REQUIRES Connect-ExchangeOnline before it can run, even though it queries the unified audit log that spans all M365 workloads. The cmdlet lives in the Exchange Online module, NOT in the Security & Compliance (IPPSSession) module. This is one of the most frequently tested SC-401 exam traps. A is wrong because Connect-IPPSSession does not expose Search-UnifiedAuditLog. C is wrong because Microsoft Graph audit cmdlets do not include Search-UnifiedAuditLog and Get-MgAuditLogSignIn is for Entra sign-ins. D is wrong because Get-ComplianceCase manages eDiscovery cases — not audit log search.

questions.stem: An eDiscovery hold is placed on a user Exchange Online mailbox as part of an eDiscovery Standard case. The user then deletes several emails and empties their Deleted Items folder. What happens to those deleted emails?
options: The emails are permanently deleted — eDiscovery holds only prevent future deletion, not items deleted after the hold is placed
The emails are preserved in the mailbox Recoverable Items folder and remain discoverable via content search within the case
The deleted emails are automatically added to the eDiscovery case review set when the user deletes them
The hold fails for newly deleted items — Litigation Hold must be used instead for prospective mailbox preservation
questions.explanation: B is correct. When an eDiscovery hold is placed on a mailbox, items the user deletes are moved to Recoverable Items → DiscoveryHolds subfolder rather than being permanently purged. They remain searchable and discoverable via content search within the case — applying both retroactively and prospectively while the hold is active. A is wrong because eDiscovery holds preserve future deletions too, not just past content. C is wrong because items are not automatically added to a review set on deletion — they are preserved in DiscoveryHolds and discoverable on demand. D is wrong because eDiscovery holds work prospectively just like Litigation Hold; both technologies preserve future deletions.

questions.stem: SharePoint content is covered by two retention policies: Policy A — Delete only after 1 year, and Policy B — Retain only for 5 years. After 1 year, what happens to the content?
options: The content is deleted by Policy A — delete actions take precedence over retain actions
The content is retained for 5 years — retention always wins over deletion for the same content
The content is retained for 5 years and then automatically deleted — both policies apply in sequence
An administrator must manually resolve the conflict before either policy takes effect
questions.explanation: B is correct. Microsoft Purview retention conflict resolution: retention wins over deletion when both apply to the same content. With Policy A (delete after 1 year) and Policy B (retain for 5 years), content is retained for the full 5 years; the 1-year deletion is suppressed. After 5 years, the deletion can then take effect. A is wrong because the deletion does NOT trump the retain action. C is wrong because the policies do not 'apply in sequence' — retain wins outright during overlap. D is wrong because retention conflicts are resolved automatically per documented rules; no admin intervention is required.

questions.stem: A retention policy covers Microsoft Teams channel messages for 3 years. A user deletes a channel message. Where is the deleted message preserved?
options: In the team connected SharePoint Preservation Hold Library
In the deleting user Exchange Online Recoverable Items folder
In a hidden SubstrateHolds folder within the team Exchange Online group mailbox
In the eDiscovery case hold container within the Microsoft Purview portal
questions.explanation: C is correct. Teams channel messages are stored in the team's Exchange Online group mailbox. When a retention policy applies and a message is deleted, the message is moved to the hidden SubstrateHolds folder within Recoverable Items of the group mailbox. This hidden folder is not user-accessible but is discoverable through eDiscovery. A is wrong because the SharePoint Preservation Hold Library preserves files in the connected SharePoint site, not Teams chat messages. B is wrong because Teams channel messages are not retained in the deleting user's personal mailbox. D is wrong because the eDiscovery case hold container is the search/result space, not the underlying preservation location.

questions.stem: A compliance admin wants to run a content search that includes an inactive mailbox (belonging to a user whose account was deleted 6 months ago). Which parameter is required?
options: -InactiveMailboxOnly $true
-IncludeInactiveMailboxes $true
-AllowNotFoundExchangeLocationsEnabled $true
-ExchangeLocation InactiveMailboxes
questions.explanation: C is correct. When adding inactive mailboxes (or other Exchange locations that do not have an active user mailbox) to a content search via PowerShell, you must include -AllowNotFoundExchangeLocationsEnabled $true on New-ComplianceSearch or Set-ComplianceSearch. Without it, specifying an inactive mailbox SMTP address returns an error because Exchange cannot find an active mailbox at that address. A is wrong because there is no -InactiveMailboxOnly parameter. B is wrong because -IncludeInactiveMailboxes is not the correct switch. D is wrong because -ExchangeLocation InactiveMailboxes is not a valid syntax.

questions.stem: A Confidential sensitivity label has a header text CONFIDENTIAL — DO NOT DISTRIBUTE but no encryption configured. Can a user delete the header text from the document?
options: No — sensitivity label visual markings cannot be modified or deleted while the label remains applied
Yes — visual markings are document text content; users can manually delete the header without removing the label
Yes — but Office automatically restores the header the next time the document is saved with the label
No — deleting the header triggers automatic label removal and a mandatory re-labeling prompt
questions.explanation: B is correct. Visual content markings (headers, footers, watermarks) are inserted into the document as text — they are NOT technically enforced. Without encryption, a user can manually select and delete the header text without removing the sensitivity label itself. For enforceable protection, encryption (not just content markings) is required. A is wrong because visual markings can be modified by users on labels that lack encryption. C is wrong because Office does not auto-restore deleted markings on save unless the label settings are re-applied — and on save, the markings are re-inserted only in the way Office applies the label at that moment. D is wrong because no automatic label removal happens when a header is deleted.

questions.stem: For Microsoft Purview to capture Microsoft 365 Copilot interaction events in the unified audit log, what is required?
options: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint deployed on all devices used with Copilot
Unified audit logging must be enabled in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal
DSPM for AI must have an active policy configured before Copilot events are logged
Microsoft 365 E5 Advanced Audit licensing is required for all Copilot event types
questions.explanation: B is correct. Copilot interaction events (CopilotInteraction record type) are captured in the unified audit log when unified audit logging is enabled — which is on by default for most M365 tenants. Basic Copilot events are captured at the Standard Audit tier. A is wrong because MDE on all devices is unrelated to Copilot service-side audit logging. C is wrong because DSPM for AI is not a prerequisite for audit log capture — it consumes audit data but doesn't unlock it. D is wrong because E5 Advanced Audit is not required for basic Copilot interaction events (although Premium events would need it).

questions.stem: An auto-labeling policy is actively applying the Internal sensitivity label (no encryption) to Exchange emails. You update the Internal label to add Assign permissions now encryption. What happens to future emails matched by the policy?
options: The auto-labeling policy stops functioning until the admin re-enables it with the updated label settings
Future matched emails will have the updated Internal label applied — including the new encryption settings
Future emails continue receiving the old Internal label configuration for 72 hours during the policy cache refresh
The policy must be deleted and recreated referencing the updated label to use the new configuration
questions.explanation: B is correct. Auto-labeling policies reference labels by identity. When the underlying label configuration is updated (e.g., adding encryption), the policy automatically uses the new settings for new applications — no policy reconfiguration required. The encryption takes effect for emails newly matched after the label-change propagates. A is wrong because the policy does not stop functioning when the label is updated. C is wrong because there is no 72-hour cache window that uses the old configuration. D is wrong because policy deletion/recreation is unnecessary — references are by identity.

questions.stem: A compliance officer uses Content Explorer and sees that 18,432 SharePoint items currently carry the Strictly Confidential sensitivity label. What does this count represent?
options: The number of times the Strictly Confidential label was applied or changed in the past 30 days
The number of SharePoint items that currently carry the Strictly Confidential sensitivity label
The number of DLP policy rule matches involving Strictly Confidential labeled items
The number of unique users who have ever applied the Strictly Confidential label
questions.explanation: B is correct. Content Explorer shows the CURRENT inventory of labeled items — 18,432 SharePoint items currently carry the Strictly Confidential label. It is a snapshot of current state. A is wrong because Content Explorer is not a 30-day event count — that is what Activity Explorer surfaces. C is wrong because DLP rule match counts are surfaced in DLP reports and Activity Explorer, not Content Explorer. D is wrong because unique-applier counts are not what Content Explorer reports.

questions.stem: You want a Proprietary Research retention label to auto-apply to documents that resemble research reports, without relying on specific keywords or consistent content patterns. Which auto-apply trigger should you use?
options: Auto-apply using a KQL keyword query searching for research-related terminology
Auto-apply using a sensitive information type matching research report patterns
Auto-apply using a trainable classifier trained on example research report documents
Auto-apply triggered by event-based retention with a research completion event type
questions.explanation: C is correct. Trainable classifiers use ML to identify content based on training examples — ideal when content has variable structure and no consistent keyword or data pattern, like research reports that share a topic and style but not a fixed format. A (KQL) is wrong because no specific keyword set is reliable — research reports vary in terminology. B (SIT) is wrong because research reports lack a structured data pattern a SIT could match. D (event-based) is wrong because event-based retention starts the clock from an event but does not auto-apply to content based on content similarity.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a DLP alert and a DLP report in Microsoft Purview?
options: DLP alerts are generated per user; DLP reports are generated per content location
DLP alerts notify admins of specific rule matches in near real time; DLP reports provide aggregated historical views of DLP activity and trends
DLP reports are available only with Microsoft 365 E5 licensing; DLP alerts require only E3
DLP alerts cover Exchange Online only; DLP reports aggregate activity across all DLP-enabled workloads
questions.explanation: B is correct. DLP alerts are near-real-time notifications about specific rule matches — providing incident-specific detail for investigation. DLP reports (in the Purview portal under Reports) provide aggregated historical views: trend charts, top matched rules, top content locations, and policy match volumes. Alerts are for incident response; reports are for trend analysis. A is wrong because alert vs report is not split by user vs location. C is wrong because both alerts and reports are available regardless of license tier (subject to feature licensing). D is wrong because DLP alerts and reports both cover all DLP-enabled workloads.

questions.stem: Information Barriers policies in Microsoft 365 restrict communication and collaboration in which workloads?
options: Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, and OneDrive for Business (plus Exchange Online when configured)
Microsoft Teams and SharePoint Online only — OneDrive and Exchange are not supported
Microsoft Teams only — Exchange and SharePoint have separate built-in isolation controls
All Microsoft 365 workloads including Power BI, Dynamics 365, and Microsoft Viva
questions.explanation: A is correct. Information Barriers enforce communication and collaboration restrictions in: Microsoft Teams (chat and channels), SharePoint Online (sharing), and OneDrive for Business (sharing). Exchange Online can also be configured to enforce IB email restrictions. B is wrong because OneDrive IS supported (and Exchange can be configured). C is wrong because IB extends beyond Teams. D is wrong because IB does not directly enforce in Power BI, Dynamics 365, or Viva — those are not standard IB-enforced workloads.

questions.stem: Which role group must a user belong to in order to create and manage Communication Compliance policies in Microsoft Purview?
options: eDiscovery Manager
Compliance Administrator or Communication Compliance Admin
Records Management
Information Protection Admin
questions.explanation: B is correct. Creating and managing Communication Compliance policies requires the Communication Compliance Admin role group (or higher: Compliance Administrator, Global Administrator). A (eDiscovery Manager) is wrong because eDiscovery rights do not include CC policy creation. C (Records Management) is wrong because that role manages retention/records, not CC. D (Information Protection Admin) is wrong because that role manages sensitivity labels, not CC policies.

questions.stem: What is a key difference between Exchange Online Litigation Hold and a Microsoft Purview retention policy applied to Exchange mailboxes?
options: Litigation Hold preserves all mailbox content indefinitely regardless of age; retention policies require a defined time period
Litigation Hold is configured per individual mailbox; retention policies can target all mailboxes at scale with a single policy
Retention policies preserve content for eDiscovery; Litigation Hold preserves content only for legal proceedings
Only retention policies are searchable via Content Search; Litigation Hold content is not discoverable
questions.explanation: B is correct. Litigation Hold is configured per individual mailbox via Exchange Online PowerShell (Set-Mailbox -LitigationHoldEnabled $true) and applies only to that mailbox. Retention policies can target mailboxes at scale — all users, static-scope user lists, or dynamic adaptive scopes — with a single policy. Both preserve content for eDiscovery, but retention policies scale more efficiently. A is wrong because Litigation Hold and retention policies can both preserve content indefinitely or for a defined period — duration is configurable in both. C is wrong because both preserve content for eDiscovery — they are not differentiated by 'compliance vs litigation' purpose. D is wrong because both retention policies and Litigation Hold content are searchable via Content Search.

questions.stem: A Communication Compliance policy has 50 specific users in the supervised population. Two supervised users exchange messages with each other. Are those messages captured by the policy?
options: Only messages FROM supervised users TO non-supervised users are captured
Messages between two supervised users ARE captured — all inbound, outbound, and internal communications for supervised users are in scope
Only one message per conversation pair is sampled daily to limit captured volume
Messages between supervised users in the same department are excluded by default
questions.explanation: B is correct. Communication Compliance captures inbound, outbound, AND internal communications for supervised users. Messages exchanged between two supervised users are fully in scope — the policy captures the complete communication universe of supervised users. A is wrong because internal messages between supervised users ARE captured, not excluded. C is wrong because there is no daily one-message sampling — the policy captures messages per its conditions. D is wrong because same-department supervised users are NOT excluded by default.

questions.stem: A Compliance Manager assessment shows a score of 420/1000 for GDPR. What does this score primarily reflect?
options: The number of GDPR articles Litware is fully compliant with out of 1,000 regulatory articles
The weighted percentage of GDPR improvement actions that have been implemented and validated
The estimated dollar value of potential GDPR fines avoided through current compliance controls
The number of days since the last GDPR-related data breach was reported to the supervisory authority
questions.explanation: B is correct. Compliance Manager scores reflect the weighted percentage of improvement actions implemented and validated, mapped to the selected regulation. Each action carries a point value based on risk impact and control importance. A higher score means more controls are implemented. A is wrong because the score is not a count of articles complied with — it is action-implementation weighted. C is wrong because the score is not a financial fine estimate. D is wrong because the score does not reflect time since last breach.

questions.stem: Before activating a new auto-labeling policy for Exchange Online in production, what should you do first to validate the policy scope and accuracy?
options: Deploy the policy to a single pilot mailbox using a static scope before expanding
Enable the policy in simulation mode and review the matched items report before turning on enforcement
Configure a low instance count threshold and gradually raise it after initial deployment
Run the policy against the previous 90 days of email using the historical analysis setting
questions.explanation: B is correct. Auto-labeling policies include a simulation mode that runs against existing content and reports what WOULD be labeled — without applying any labels. Reviewing simulation results lets admins assess accuracy (false positives and false negatives), refine conditions, and only then enable enforcement. A (pilot mailbox with static scope) is wrong because static scoping doesn't show the policy's accuracy against the broader content set — simulation does. C (low instance count threshold) is wrong because that affects which items match, not whether the policy applies labels. D (historical 90-day analysis) is wrong because such a setting is not part of auto-labeling configuration — simulation mode is the right tool.

questions.stem: The Search-UnifiedAuditLog command requires Connect-ExchangeOnline to be run first before it executes successfully.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Search-UnifiedAuditLog is an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet — Connect-ExchangeOnline must be established before running it. Despite querying the unified audit log that spans all M365 workloads, the cmdlet belongs to the Exchange Online PowerShell module. Connect-IPPSSession does NOT give access to this cmdlet — a frequently tested SC-401 trap. No would be wrong because it implies a different connection works, which is incorrect.

questions.stem: The command as written retrieves audit events across ALL Microsoft 365 workloads within the specified date range.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. The -RecordType SharePointFileOperation parameter limits results to SharePoint file operation events; -Operations FileAccessed further narrows to file-access events specifically. The command does NOT retrieve events across all workloads — it is scoped to SharePoint FileAccessed only. Yes would be wrong because it ignores the explicit -RecordType and -Operations filters.

questions.stem: With Microsoft 365 E5 licenses assigned, users audit logs are retained for 1 year by default without any custom audit retention policy.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Microsoft 365 E5 (and E5 Compliance) provides 1-year default audit log retention for licensed users — an upgrade from the 90-day default included with E3. Custom audit retention policies can extend this further, up to 10 years with the 10-Year Audit Retention add-on. No would be wrong because 90 days is the E3 default, not E5.

questions.stem: The 5-year custom SharePoint retention policy takes precedence over the 90-day default org-wide policy for the same SharePoint content.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. When multiple retention policies apply to the same content, the longest retention period wins (retain longer beats dispose sooner). The explicit 5-year custom policy also takes precedence over the org-wide 90-day default policy — content will be retained for 5 years. No would be wrong because retention conflict rules favor the longer retention.

questions.stem: To extend audit retention to 10 years for specific users, assigning a Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance license is sufficient — no additional license is required.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. E5 and E5 Compliance provide 1-year default audit retention. Extending audit retention to 10 years requires BOTH an E5 (or E5 Compliance) license AND the separate Microsoft Purview Audit (Premium) 10-Year Retention add-on license. E5 alone is not sufficient. Yes would be wrong because it omits the required add-on.

questions.stem: A user must have the Audit Logs role in Exchange Online or the Compliance Administrator role to run Search-UnifiedAuditLog successfully.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Running Search-UnifiedAuditLog requires the View-Only Audit Logs or Audit Logs role assigned in Exchange Online (or a higher role like Compliance Administrator or Global Administrator that includes these rights). Without the role, the cmdlet returns empty results or an access-denied error even after Connect-ExchangeOnline succeeds. No would be wrong because role assignment is required in addition to the connection.
